title: Absolute liability — M.C. Mehta (Oleum Gas Leak)

content.overview: Absolute liability, formulated in M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak), holds that an enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous activity owes an absolute and non-delegable duty to the community. Escape of a hazardous substance attracting this rule does not admit the Rylands exceptions. Compensation is correlated to the magnitude and capacity of the enterprise.

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: Justice P.N. Bhagwati's formulation responds to industrial risk in Indian conditions. Where the activity is hazardous or inherently dangerous, the enterprise must absorb the cost of harm from that activity. The duty is non-delegable.

sections.heading: No Rylands exceptions
sections.body: Act of God, stranger, and related Rylands exceptions do not dilute absolute liability once the rule applies. That is the doctrinal break from strict liability.

sections.heading: Measure of compensation
sections.body: Compensation should reflect the enterprise's magnitude and capacity — a deterrent and restorative measure suited to large hazardous industries, not a purely nominal figure.

sections.heading: Track B
sections.body: Frame pleadings around hazardous activity, control by the enterprise, escape/harm, and community injury. Cite M.C. Mehta for the rule; do not invent paragraph numbers. Parallel public-law remedies under Articles 32/226 may coexist in appropriate facts (constitutional tort / public law compensation).

enhancement.definition: Absolute liability is the Indian rule that an enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous activity has an absolute and non-delegable duty to ensure that no harm results from that activity.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: For hazardous industries, the Supreme Court developed a stricter rule than Rylands v Fletcher, without the traditional exceptions.
enhancement.statutoryFramework: Indian tort law is largely uncodified. The governing rules are developed through common-law principles, Indian judicial decisions and applicable legislation for particular fields.

notes: Opened https://api.sci.gov.in/jonew/judis/7699.pdf. It is Charan Lal Sahu v. Union of India, judgment dated 22/12/1989 (1990 AIR 1480; 1990 SCC (1) 613), not the Oleum Gas Leak judgment.
That official text quotes the M.C. Mehta absolute and non-delegable liability formulation and states that the quoted law made a landmark departure from the exceptions to Rylands v. Fletcher.
The original M.C. Mehta Oleum judgment was not opened in this pass. The topic therefore remains in-progress and is not marked verified or published.

No new statutory provision was invented. Absolute liability remains a judicial doctrine, later interfacing with statutes such as the Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991, which was not re-verified in this pass.

Fletcher. The original Oleum judgment PDF was not opened in this pass, so this entry remains pending direct verification.

caseLaw.name: Charan Lal Sahu v. Union of India
caseLaw.holding: Official Supreme Court text quotes the M.C. Mehta formulation: an enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous activity owes an absolute and non-delegable duty, and is strictly and absolutely liable to compensate those affected by an accident such as escape of toxic gas, not subject to the exceptions which operate under Rylands v. Fletcher.
